title: The 90% Problem in Web Search Benchmarks | NewsCatcher
summary: Every search API now scores 90% on web search benchmarks, so they can't tell you which to buy. Here's the 90% problem, and how we measure recall instead.
body_markdown:
Every search API scores 90%, so the benchmarks can't tell you which one to buy. Here's what we measure instead: the events you'd miss.


**TL;DR:**


- Most web search benchmarks ask a question with one known answer and check whether the answer came back. Every serious provider now scores 91–97% on them, so they no longer tell you which API to buy. That’s the 90% problem.
- We built a news search benchmark that also measures recall: of all the real events that happened, how many did one search surface?
- Precision is enough when you need one good answer. Recall is the metric for the business jobs where a missed event costs money: deal sourcing, adverse media, supplier risk, lead lists.
- In the first run of our recall test (November 17, 2026), no system found even half of the events. The best one found 43%.
- At 50 results, 1,000 distinct events cost $0.37–$0.56 with NewsCatcher at medium and high effort ($0.07 at low) and $3.41–$3.86 with Exa. At 10 results, Exa’s cheapest tier is cheaper per event than our default.
- We put recall and duplicates ahead of speed. Our deepest search takes about 14 seconds, and in return it finds about a third more events than our default and repeats far less. For a monitoring job nobody is waiting on, that’s the right trade; for a chat box it isn’t, and we say so.


## The 90% problem in search API benchmarks


There’s a quiet consensus in search API marketing: everyone is excellent.


- **SimpleQA:** Parallel’s own comparison puts the leading providers at 91% to 97% on SimpleQA Verified, a set of short fact questions with one verifiable answer each ([Parallel](https://parallel.ai/articles/simpleqa-benchmark) ).
- **An independent rerun:** 1,000 of those questions found the top three providers within the margin of error of one another, between 96.9% and 97.8% ([cloro](https://cloro.dev/blog/web-search-api-benchmark/) ).


When everyone scores 97%, the benchmark has stopped measuring the systems. It has started measuring itself.


We saw the same thing in our own data. Our everyday search benchmark, S2, sends 60 ordinary queries to eight systems: company names, topics, questions, a single story and non-English queries. The rule that makes it easy is one most benchmarks use by default: every relevant article counts, even if it’s the fifth article about the same story.


- **Ranking quality** (nDCG@10, 1 = a perfect top 10): every API vendor we tested scored between 0.79 and 0.87.
- **Single-story queries:** every system found the target story in its top 10, 100% of the time.
- **Question queries:** every system had an answering article somewhere in its top 10 on 92–100% of questions.
- **The judge:** it gave the top grade to 72% of everything in a top 10.


By that measure, every news search API is roughly as good as every other. That’s true for one job: getting a decent first page for an ordinary query. It’s false for the job our customers pay for.


The gap between those two jobs is the gap between precision and recall.


## Precision vs recall, in plain terms


**Precision** asks: of what the system returned, how much was right?


- If a search for “Series B rounds in healthcare” returns 20 articles and 10 report an actual healthcare Series B inside the date window, precision at 20 (P@20) is 0.50.


**Recall** asks: of everything that should have come back, how much did?


- If 40 healthcare companies announced a Series B that month and the search surfaced 12 of them, recall is 0.30.


The two answer different questions, and a system can be excellent at one and poor at the other. A search that returns three perfect articles has perfect precision and terrible recall. A search that returns everything ever published has perfect recall and useless precision.


Two details decide whether either number means anything.


### Count events, not articles


Five articles about the same funding round aren’t five answers. They’re one answer, repeated. A benchmark that counts articles rewards an engine for returning the same story over and over.


- **In S1, our recall benchmark,** one provider’s article-level P@20 was 0.65. Counted by distinct events, it fell to 0.49: about a quarter of its good results repeated an event it had already shown.
- **Our own drop was 0.51 to 0.48,** because our search groups articles about the same story.


Whether you count articles or events decides who looks better at the top of the list.


### Recall needs a denominator


Precision is easy to measure: judge what came back. Recall is hard, because you need to know what *should* have come back, and nobody has a complete list of every Series B announced last month.


The standard answer comes from TREC, the long-running information retrieval evaluation run by NIST:


- **Pool** the results of every system being compared, judge them all, and treat the union of correct answers as the ground truth.
- **The known flaw:** pooled recall overstates absolute recall, since some real events are found by no system.
- **Why it still works:** research on TREC collections found that the relative ranking of systems holds up ([Zobel, SIGIR 1998](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs574/2002fa/assignments.org/zobel-sigir98.pdf) ).


So our recall numbers mean “share of the events that any system found”, and we say so.


## Precision is enough for nice-to-have use cases


Plenty of products need precision and little else.


- **A chat assistant answering “what happened with Nvidia this week?”** needs two or three good sources. The 40th relevant article adds nothing.
- **A news widget on a company profile page** needs a clean top five.
- **An answer engine** needs the article that states the answer, ranked first.


For these jobs the right metrics are precision at the top and whether the answer appears at rank 1. That’s what S2 measures, and the result is honest: on question queries, Exa put an answering article first more often than we did (92% of questions for Exa’s` auto` mode, 67% for ours).


If your product is a chatbot that cites three links, a precision benchmark is the right one to read. A missed event costs you little, because nobody notices it.


## Recall is what business users need


Our enterprise customers mostly don’t ask questions. They watch a class of events and need every instance of it.


- **Deal sourcing:** every seed and Series A round in climate tech this month, because each one missed is a company a competitor calls first.
- **Adverse media and KYC:** every negative story about a counterparty: fines, sanctions, lawsuits, fraud allegations. The one story you miss is the one the regulator asks about.
- **Supplier and supply chain risk:** every plant closure, recall, strike or bankruptcy among 5,000 suppliers. Missing one can stop a production line.
- **Credit and market risk:** every rating downgrade, profit warning and executive departure across a portfolio.
- **Lead lists and market maps:** every company that just raised, hired a new CFO or opened a European office.


These jobs share an asymmetry that precision benchmarks hide.


- **A false positive is visible and cheap.** An analyst or a language model reads an irrelevant row and drops it in seconds. Filtering 50 results with an LLM costs a fraction of a cent.
- **A false negative is invisible and expensive.** Nobody reviews the event that never came back. You only find out when the deal closes without you, or the auditor finds the story.


Precision can be bought after retrieval. You can rerank, filter, deduplicate and verify what you have. Recall can’t: no amount of post-processing recovers an event the search never returned. That’s why our recall benchmark, S1, is the one we built our news search around.


## How we benchmark news search for recall


S1 asks one buyer’s question: *I watch a class of events. When I search for it over the last day, week or month, how many of the real events does one search bring back, and how much of what comes back is right?*


### The queries


- **50 event classes,** written for the benchmark, covering funding, M&A, leadership changes, layoffs, expansion, regulation, legal action, risk and capital markets. Examples: “seed rounds”, “CEO changes in fintech”, “product recalls”, “ransomware attacks on hospitals”, “IPO filings”.
- **Three windows each:** the last 24 hours, 7 days and 30 days. That’s 150 query-windows.
- **No query tuned to any vendor.** Where a vendor’s documentation asks for a different query shape, we apply one fixed template to all 50.


### The systems, and why each setting


**The rule:**


- Every provider runs in the setting its own documentation recommends for this job: news about a class of events in a time window, with as many distinct events as possible in one call.
- Every setting is a public, documented option. We checked each with one live call before the run.
- No query is tuned per vendor. Where a vendor’s docs ask for a different query shape, one fixed template applies to all 50 queries.


System Setting Why this one


**NewsCatcher` medium`**` /search` ,` effort=medium` ,` collapse=story` , 50 results Our default effort.` collapse=story` returns one article per story, our documented setting for the most distinct events per result.


NewsCatcher` low` and` high` the same, with` effort=low` /` high` Our other two levels:` low` is the raw ranking, the cheapest and fastest;` high` adds an LLM judgement and merges stories about the same event. We show all three so you see what each costs and buys.


NewsCatcher` medium` , English only the same, with` languages=en` About a quarter of our default results are in other languages, and a judge reading English titles could penalize that. This variant checks it: the score barely moved.


**Exa` auto`**` /search` ,` type=auto` , news category, publication-date filter, query “news articles about {query}”, 50 results Exa’s documented default for most applications. Its docs say to describe the pages you want and to use date filters for a time window, so we did both.


Exa` lite` the same, with` type=lite` Exa’s low-cost, low-latency tier, which replaces its older` instant` and` fast` types (now marked legacy). It turned out to be Exa’s best mode on this test.


**Parallel` advanced`** Search API,` mode=advanced` , a goal-style objective plus the query, start date set to the window, 20 results Parallel’s highest-quality search mode. Its evaluation guide recommends a goal-style objective with short keyword queries. Its public search returns at most 20 results.


Parallel` basic` the same, with` mode=basic` The mode Parallel’s guide suggests as a starting point for evaluations.


**Firecrawl news**` /v2/search` , news source, 50 results Firecrawl’s news source. Its time filter applies only to web results, so the window is enforced at scoring: out-of-window results count as misses. Its web source with a time filter was tested and dropped, because it returned undated general pages rather than news.


**Google News** RSS search with` when:` set to the window, US English A reference, not a product under test: free, widely used, and an independent source of events for the recall pool. It isn’t priced.


**Also:**


- **Same moment:** every system for a query-window was called within the same seconds, so nobody gets fresher news.
- **Not tested in this run:** Exa’s` deep` and` deep-lite` search types. They do multi-step research before returning results and could raise Exa’s recall. They’re the obvious candidates for the next run.
- **S2 uses the same settings,** at 10 results per call.


### The judging


- **Blind and pooled:** every unique result across all systems went into one shuffled pool, with system names hidden. That came to 35,075 results.
- **The judge:** Claude Opus 5.5 labelled each result: is it an instance of the event class; is it real news, not a listing, profile or SEO page; which real-world event does it report.
- **What the judge sees:** each result’s title, site and date. We fetch the pages to check their dates, but the judge works from the headline, which is roughly what a person scanning a result list sees.
- **Grouping:** a second pass grouped results about the same event, so ten articles about one round count once.
- **Dates:** we fetched over 20,000 cited pages to check their real publication date. An old article labelled as recent counts as outside the window.
- **The denominator:** recall is measured against every event found by any system’s top 50, plus Google News’s top 100. 147 query-windows had enough events to score. They held 6,034 distinct events, 41 per query-window on average.
- **Statistics:** every difference carries a paired 95% bootstrap interval. If the interval crosses zero, we call it a tie.


### The shortcuts we don’t take


Each of these would raise every provider’s score, including ours.


1. **Questions with one known answer.** They measure whether the answer is in the top 10. On news, it nearly always is.
2. **Counting articles instead of events.** Repeats inflate precision for engines that don’t group stories.
3. **Judging only the top 10.** A top 10 can’t hold 41 events. In our first run, no system’s top 10 held more than 20% of the events.
4. **Trusting the system’s own dates.** We checked every cited page we could read. 17–19% of one provider’s dates were more than three days off the page’s own date, nearly always an old article shown as recent. Ours were off 0.1–0.2% of the time. Wrong dates inflate freshness and relevance at the same time.
5. **A lenient relevance bar.** “About the topic” isn’t “an instance of the event”. A piece on funding trends in healthcare isn’t a Series B.


## What the first run showed


These numbers come from our first run, on November 17, 2026. We repeat the same 50 searches in mid-December, on fresh news, to check that they hold. Each distinct event counts once.


System P@10 P@20 P@50 Recall@50, per search Recall@50, all events Events in top 50 Repeats Non-news


NewsCatcher, high 0.52 0.48 0.36 0.43 0.43 17.8 4% 2%


NewsCatcher, medium (default) 0.49 0.41 0.27 0.32 0.33 13.5 7% 3%


Exa, lite 0.63 0.49 0.26 0.37 0.31 12.9 16% 11%


Exa, auto 0.61 0.49 0.24 0.35 0.30 12.2 15% 13%


Parallel, advanced (20 max) 0.48 0.39 n/a n/a n/a n/a 18% 16%


Firecrawl, news 0.12 0.10 0.06 0.07 0.08 3.2 7% 18%


Google News (reference) 0.25 0.24 0.15 0.19 0.18 7.5 15% 15%


147 query-windows; a query-window is one query searched over one time window. Recall is measured against all events found by any system.


**Why there are two recall columns.** They count the same events in two ways, and they can disagree:


- **Per search:** each search’s recall is a share (events found ÷ events that exist for that search), and the shares are averaged. A narrow search with 7 events counts as much as a broad one with 106. This is the standard in search evaluation, and it’s our headline.
- **All events:** every event from every search goes into one pool, and we count how many each system found. Broad searches weigh more because they hold more events.


**An example:**


- “Founders stepping down as CEO”, last 7 days: 7 events existed. Exa found 5 (71%), our` medium` found 2 (29%).
- “New CFO appointments”, last 30 days: 106 events existed. Our` medium` found 41 (39%), Exa found 20 (19%).
- Per search, Exa’s three extra events in the small search outweigh our 21 extra events in the big one. Counted across all events, ours count more.


That’s how our default` medium` finds more events in total (13.5 vs 12.9 per search) while trailing Exa lite on per-search recall. Exa is stronger on narrow event classes with few events; we’re stronger on broad ones. Our` high` effort leads both ways.


Four things stand out.


**1. Nobody finds half the events.**


- The best configuration found 43% of the pooled events in its top 50. The best competitor found 37%.
- The average query-window held 41 distinct events, so a perfect top 50 would have had room for nearly all of them. 29% held more than 50.
- That’s the real state of news search for monitoring, and precision benchmarks never show it.


**2. Precision at the top and recall at depth point in opposite directions.**


- **Top 10:** Exa’s results are more precise than ours (0.63 vs 0.52 distinct-event P@10, an interval of −0.15 to −0.06).
- **Top 20:** a tie (0.49 vs 0.48). We won 66 query-windows, tied 16 and lost 65.
- **Top 50:** we’re ahead on precision (0.36 vs 0.26) and on recall (0.43 vs 0.37, +0.06 \[+0.01, +0.10\]).
- **Events per search:** our high effort surfaced about five more distinct events per search (+4.9 \[+3.1, +6.6\]).
- A benchmark that stops at 10 results would tell you to buy the other product. One that measures the job tells you something more useful.


**3. The longer the window, the wider the gap.**


- Recall@50 at 30 days: NewsCatcher high 0.49, Exa lite 0.27.
- At 7 days we lead by 9 points. In the last 24 hours Exa leads by 14.
- Monitoring workloads are mostly weekly and monthly sweeps, which is where the difference shows.


**4. Clean results are cheaper results.**


- Our top 50 repeated an event 4–7% of the time and held 2–3% non-news, against 15–16% and 11–13% for Exa.
- Fewer repeats mean more distinct events per search, and we charge per search, not per result. “What it costs”, below, has the numbers.


## The same discipline, applied to everyday search


S2 is our precision benchmark, and we score it with the same rule: each story counts once.


- **The setup:** 60 everyday queries, 90 query-windows, each system’s top 10, graded 0–3 by the same blind judge. Firecrawl isn’t scored here: its run didn’t complete.
- **Counted by article,** the field is flat: 0.79–0.87 nDCG@10 for every API vendor.
- **Counted by story,** it separates: NewsCatcher high 0.82, NewsCatcher medium 0.69, Exa lite 0.64, Exa auto 0.63, Parallel 0.53–0.54, Google News 0.45. NewsCatcher high beat Exa on 76 of 90 query-windows (+0.18 \[+0.14, +0.22\]). The lead comes from variety: 13% of its top 10 repeated a story, against 38–39% for Exa.

**How to read it:**


- **Our price doesn’t change with depth,** so the further down you read, the cheaper each event gets. Exa’s price rises with depth while its new events dry up after about 30 results, so each event gets more expensive.
- **At 50 results,** 1,000 distinct events cost $0.37–$0.56 with us against $3.41–$3.86 with Exa: 6 to 10 times less.
- **At 10 results, Exa lite is cheaper per event** than our` medium` and` high` : its base price covers 10 results, and its top 10 is sharper.
- **Our` low` is the cheapest at every depth,** but it finds fewer events per search: 3.9 in the top 10, against Exa lite’s 6.3.


### Everyday search, 10 results


For ordinary queries at 10 results, the size of a chat answer, the price picture is different: Exa lite buys good stories more cheaply than our default. That comparison is the subject of a companion post, **The Price of a Good First Page** .


### A monitoring budget


A team that searches 200 event classes every morning, reading 50 results each time, runs 6,000 searches a month:


- **NewsCatcher:** $30 at` medium` , $60 at` high` .
- **Exa:** $264 at` lite` , $282 at` auto` .
- **Parallel** can’t return 50 results.


Per search,` high` returns 17.8 distinct events, against 12.9 for Exa lite.


### What the benchmark itself costs


- **S1, one run:** about $21 of searches across all ten configurations, and about $70 for the judge (35,000 results).
- **S2, one run:** $3.33 of searches and $17.82 for the judge.


Anyone with API keys can rerun either one for less than $100.


## Why recall and duplicates come before speed


Speed is the easiest number to benchmark and the easiest to sell. We report it in every table, but we don’t optimize our headline for it. Here’s why.


### What the extra seconds buy


Our search has three effort levels, and the[docs](https://www.newscatcherapi.com/docs/news/effort-levels) say exactly what each one adds:


- **` low`** returns the first ranking as is.
- **` medium`** (the default) reranks the top stories with a cross-encoder.
- **` high`** has an LLM judge the top stories and merges stories that report the same event.


In S1,` high` takes 13.5 seconds at the median, against 2.2 for` medium` . On the same index and the same queries, the extra 11 seconds buy:


- **Recall@50:** 0.43 instead of 0.32.
- **Distinct events in the top 50:** 17.8 instead of 13.5.
- **Repeats:** 4% of the top 50 instead of 7%. In S2, 13% of the top 10 instead of 32%.
- **Ranking quality in S2** (nDCG@10, each story once): 0.82 instead of 0.69.


The fastest tiers on the market answer in half a second partly because they skip work at query time. Exa[documents](https://exa.ai/docs/reference/search.md) its` lite` tier as serving straight from its index, without fetching pages when you search. That’s a sound design for a chat box, and it’s a trade-off, not a free lunch.


### Who is waiting for the search?


- **In a chat or voice assistant, a person is.** Every second shows, and latency should weigh heavily in your choice. Our` low` and` medium` efforts answer in about 2–3 seconds; sub-second tiers exist elsewhere, and we say so below.
- **In a monitoring job, nobody is.** A deal team’s morning sweep over 200 event classes runs in the background. At 14 seconds a search and 10 searches at a time, it’s done in under five minutes.
- **The two costs aren’t the same size.** Latency is paid once, when the search runs. A missed event keeps costing you for as long as nobody knows about it: the deal you didn’t call, the supplier risk you didn’t flag.


### Why duplicates matter as much as recall


- **A repeat takes the place of an event you didn’t get.** If 4 of your top 10 results repeat a story already shown, you have 6 answers, not 10. In S2, 38–39% of Exa’s top-10 results repeated a story it had already returned. For our` high` effort it was 13%.
- **Repeats cost money after the search.** An analyst reads them, an LLM spends tokens on them, an index stores them. In a pipeline that summarises every result, a third of the reading budget can go on stories you already have.
- **Repeats flatter benchmarks.** Counted by article, they look like precision. Research on TREC’s test collections found that ignoring duplicates inflates scores by up to 17% and reorders systems by up to 53 places ([Fröbe et al., ECIR 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7148013) ). Systems that filter duplicates are the ones penalized.


That’s why the repeat share is its own column in every table, and why our headline metrics give a repeat no credit.


## Where we lose


A benchmark that a vendor always wins isn’t worth reading.


- **Top-10 precision on event queries.** Exa’s first 10 results are more precise.
- **The last 24 hours.** Exa finds more of today’s events (recall@50 −0.14).
- **Our default effort level.**` medium` doesn’t beat Exa on per-search recall@50 (0.32 vs 0.37) or on P@20 (0.41 vs 0.49). Counted across all events it’s slightly ahead (0.33 vs 0.31), but the gap on narrow searches is real. The clear recall lead belongs to` high` . If recall is your job, use` high` .
- **Speed.**` high` takes about 14 seconds at the median in S2; Exa lite takes half a second. For an answer engine in a chat loop, that matters. It’s a trade we make on purpose (see above), but it’s a real loss for that use.
- **Answer at rank 1.** On question queries, Exa put the answer first more often (92% vs 67%).
- **Why our top 10 is less precise:** it isn’t junk. Our top 10 is almost all news. But 38–40% of it is only partly on topic, such as trend pieces, policy discussion and aggregators, where the other engine returns concrete instances. That’s a ranking problem we’re working on, and the next run will show whether it moved.


## How to evaluate a news API for your own use case


You don’t need our harness to run the test that matters. You need your own event classes and a spreadsheet.


1. **Write 20–50 queries in the shape of your job:** “plant closures in Germany”, “Series A in climate tech”, not “What is Nvidia’s stock price?”.
2. **Call every provider in the same minute** with each vendor’s recommended settings, asking for the depth you’ll actually use.
3. **Pool and blind** the results, then label each one: is it an instance, which event is it, and is it inside your window by the page’s own date?
4. **Count distinct events,** and measure recall against the pool.
5. **Price it per distinct event** at your depth, not per call.


The scoring is a few lines of Python:


` from collections import defaultdict


def score(results, k=50):
"""results: one dict per returned item, already labelled:
{"system": "a", "query": "seed rounds", "rank": 1,
"good": True, "event": "Acme | seed | $4M"}
Returns P@k (each event counted once) and pooled recall@k per system."""
# query -> every good event any system found
pool = defaultdict(set)
# (system, query) -> distinct good events in its top k
found = defaultdict(set)
for r in results:
if r\["good"\]:
pool\[r\["query"\]\].add(r\["event"\])
if r\["rank"\] <= k:
found\[(r\["system"\], r\["query"\])\].add(r\["event"\])
by_system = defaultdict(list)
for (system, query), events in found.items():
by_system\[system\].append((len(events) / k, len(events) / len(pool\[query\])))
queries = len(pool)
# queries where a system found nothing count as 0
return {s: {"P@k": sum(p for p, _ in v) / queries,
"recall@k": sum(r for _, r in v) / queries}
for s, v in by_system.items()}
`


## Conclusion


A benchmark where every provider scores 90% isn’t wrong. It’s measuring a job that every provider has already solved: finding one good article. The job that’s still unsolved is the one businesses pay for: finding all of them.


- In the first run, the best system found 43% of the events any system found.
- The gap between providers was largest exactly where monitoring lives: deep result lists and week-to-month windows.


We’ll publish the queries, labels and raw results with the second run, so you can check our work.
